title: Solid jobs data keeps RBA on edge over rates
full_text:
The buoyant jobs market will keep the Reserve Bank board on edge when it meets next month, and another increase to interest rates is now widely expected before Christmas.
But an eye-catching jump in monthly employment data tells only part of the story.
Employment jumped by 76,300 in June, dwarfing market expectations of a 15,000 rise. Looking beneath the surface, the data shows the jobs surge reflected an increase in labour supply.
With the participation rate soaring from 66.7 per cent to an 11-month high of 67 per cent, the unemployment rate held steady at 4.4 per cent. Still, the fact that employers found jobs for tens of thousands more people last month is impressive.
The RBA monetary policy board has repeatedly said economic growth needs to slow to get inflation down. After their last board meeting in June, members “judged the easing in growth to be broadly in line with earlier expectations”.
But the RBA’s May forecasts for economic growth only get core inflation back to the midpoint of the 2-3 per cent target in mid-2028. That forecast assumed the cash rate would hit 4.7 per cent by December 2026 – 35 basis points above the current level of 4.35 per cent. Is the economy slowing fast enough?
To be sure, there are some signs of rising slack in the labour market. The percentage of workers employed but wanting more work hit a 22-month high of 6.5 per cent, having risen sharply from a 17-year low of 5.7 per cent last December.
“It could be that the supply upturn is demand-led, with more Australians being enticed into work by still widely available job opportunities,” Betashares chief economist David Bassanese said. “But it could also reflect cost-of-living pressures forcing more Australians into the work force.” However, the latest evidence of still bountiful jobs growth – albeit possibly supply-driven – will keep the RBA on edge about possible wage pressures and firmer consumer spending.
Bassanese says next week’s CPI inflation data for the June quarter will “make or break” the case for a rate rise on August 11, with an annual trimmed mean inflation result above the RBA’s May forecast of 3.8 per cent likely to cement the case for an increase.
Inflationary pressures have been mixed in recent months.
Fuel prices have eased but new house prices and rents are likely to have risen, particularly following tax changes included in the May federal budget.
Also, while it won’t be captured in next week’s inflation data, the Middle East crisis has deteriorated this month, causing a renewed surge in oil and gas prices.
Rate-rise pricing on the money market increased after the jobs data. The market-implied chance of a 25 basis point lift after the August 10-11 meeting shot up to 36 per cent, from 20 per cent.
The chance of interest rates being lifted by December hit 100 per cent. Goldman Sachs chief economist Andrew Boak notes that RBA governor Michele Bullock recently described labour market conditions as “a bit tight” when the unemployment rate was at 4.5 per cent.
Based on that, the central bank may view the current level as tighter still. Even so, the unemployment rate averaged 20 basis points above RBA forecasts in the June quarter and underemployment has risen 60 basis points over the past two months, albeit partly due to an ABS data revision after a systems error was discovered.
Most economists say steady unemployment provides a better signal of underlying labour market conditions than the headline employment gain.
But Capital Economics senior APAC economist Abhijit Surya is more hawkish. His forecast for an August rate rise “remains alive and well”, provided next week’s CPI confirms underlying inflation accelerated sharply in the quarter.
AMP deputy chief economist Diana Mousina also expects a rate rise next month, as the jobs data give the RBA room to move with less fear of hurting the economy.
But JPMorgan senior economist Tom Kennedy says the CPI is tracking well below the RBA’s May forecast, which “pushes back on market pricing for additional policy tightening”.
CBA’s head of Australian economics Belinda Allen also expects the RBA to hold next month, albeit an upside CPI surprise – amplified by soaring oil prices – would shift that calculus. Ahead of the inflation data next Wednesday, economists and financial markets will scrutinise Bullock’s speech at the Anika Foundation on Tuesday for any signal on how the RBA is weighing rising oil prices and Middle East tensions against the inflation outlook.
